explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, that after one more plague Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “…will allow you to leave this place.” And when he lets them go, “…he will drive you out completely.” This is a king who went from holding the door shut to practically shoving everybody through it.

The LORD never says anything like that, friend. He says Pharaoh “…will allow you to leave this place.” Moses also tells Pharaoh that his officials will come and bow, saying, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” (Exodus 11:8). Half a parade is just a sad walk down the road, so I'm glad that's not the plan.

Nothing about flocks being held back shows up in this promise, baker. The LORD says, “…he will allow you to leave this place.” And when Pharaoh lets them go, “…he will drive you out completely.” Picture getting driven out the door while the one doing the driving yells, "Wait, leave the sheep!" That's not in the words the LORD gives.

Yes, baker. The LORD says “…men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold.” Everybody gets a part in it, not just a few. Asking a neighbor to borrow a ladder is awkward enough, so I'm glad nobody handed me this assignment.
Tents aren't on the list, friend. The LORD says the people should ask their neighbors for “…articles of silver and gold.” That's what He names, and the text doesn't add anything else to it.

Cattle and sheep sound like a reasonable ask, baker, but they aren't in this request. The LORD tells Moses that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold. Silver and gold are the two things He names, and livestock isn't one of them.

You've got it, baker. The text says, “And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians.” After everything Egypt has been through, that's a surprise. I think it's one more sign that the LORD is the One running this whole story.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians.” So the Israelites are about to ask their neighbors for silver and gold, and the LORD has already given them favor with those neighbors.

Right, baker. The text says Moses himself “…was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.” Think about that for a second. After all those wonders, Pharaoh's own officials still think highly of him. I'd be thrilled if a baker still thought that much of me after one burnt batch.

Not quite, friend. The text says Moses was “…highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.” That's about as far from barely known as you can get. Plenty of people in Egypt know exactly who he is.

You'd expect that, wouldn't you? But the text says the opposite: Moses was “…highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.” Respect, not mockery. Even Pharaoh's own officials are on that list.

The message says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again.” This is a heavy part of the story. It's not like any cry Egypt has heard.

That's right, baker. The message says, “Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again.” This is a heavy part of the story, so I'll just say it plainly. The cry that comes will be like nothing Egypt has ever heard.

explanations.answer: Not even a dog will snarl
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The message says, “But among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.” Dogs love to make noise, so a quiet dog is a big deal. And then, the message says, they will know the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.

explanations.answer: Not even a lamp will go out
explanations.explanation: Lamps don't come up here, friend. The message says that among all the Israelites, “…not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.” A lamp is a fair guess for a midnight scene, since the LORD does say “About midnight” (Exodus 11:4). But the message names a dog and a snarl.

explanations.answer: Not even a door will creak
explanations.explanation: A creaking door is a fair guess, but it's not in the message. What it says is that among all the Israelites, “…not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.” The message gives a dog and a snarl, not a door and a creak.

Baked right in, baker. Moses says, “Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.” A distinction means He sets one apart from the other. The people will see it for themselves.

A treaty is two sides signing on, friend, and that's not what the message says. It says, “Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.” No signatures, just the LORD setting one apart from the other.

Nobody's haggling here, baker. The message says, “Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.” A bargain is a deal between two sides, and this is the LORD speaking. The word is distinction.

explanations.answer: Go you and all your people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses tells Pharaoh his officials will come and bow before him, saying, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” Those are Pharaoh's own officials in that picture, and they're the ones bowing. Then, the text says, Moses left Pharaoh's presence hot with anger.

explanations.answer: Stay and keep working for us
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Moses says Pharaoh's officials will come and bow before him, saying, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” Officials bowing low and the first word out of their mouths is "Go." Nobody in that scene is asking anyone to stay. Then, the text says, Moses left Pharaoh's presence hot with anger.

explanations.answer: Go but leave your flocks here
explanations.explanation: That's a sneaky little add-on, baker, but it isn't in Moses' words. He says the officials will bow and say, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” It's a send-off with no fine print. You know that great deal where the tiny print at the bottom ruins everything? Not this one.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD tells Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” And the text says the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he would not let the Israelites go. So no, Pharaoh isn't listening yet.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” Moses and Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), did all the wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart anyway. The story keeps going.

explanations.answer: The first month of their year
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year.” It's a fresh start on the calendar. And it's the LORD who sets it.

explanations.answer: The last month of their year
explanations.explanation: It's the other end of the calendar, friend. The LORD says, “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year.” This month starts things off, it doesn't close them out.

explanations.answer: A month of fasting for them
explanations.explanation: No fasting here, baker. The LORD says, “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year.” Fasting is never mentioned in what He says about this month.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says that if a household is too small for a whole lamb, “…they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people…” So the lamb gets divided according to how many are eating. I think that makes for a very friendly night.

It's actually true, friend. The LORD says that a household too small for a whole lamb is “…to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people…” The lamb gets divided up according to how many are eating.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male…” Three things: no blemish, a year old, and male. I wish my dough came with instructions that clear.

explanations.answer: The biggest one in the flock
explanations.explanation: Size isn't what the LORD asks about, friend. He says, “Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male…” The word is unblemished, and nothing in the text says it has to be the biggest.
The text names an age, but not a season. The LORD says the lamb must be “…an unblemished year-old male…” Nothing is said about spring, so I won't add it.
The LORD actually leaves the door open on this one, friend. He says, “Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats.” So sheep or goats both work.
Right, baker. The LORD says the lamb may come “…from the sheep or the goats.” Both are allowed. The rule that matters is that it's an unblemished year-old male.

explanations.answer: On the doorframes of their houses
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says they “…are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs.” It goes on the sides and the top of each frame. And hold onto that blood, because it comes up again in a big way.

explanations.answer: On the horns of the altar
explanations.explanation: No altar in this one, friend. The LORD says the blood goes “…on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs.” The doorframes are the spot, not an altar.

explanations.answer: On the earlobes of the priests
explanations.explanation: That's a creative guess, baker, but earlobes aren't in this one. The LORD says the blood goes on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. Doorframes, not earlobes.

Right, baker. The LORD says, “Do not leave any of it until morning…” The meal is for that night, so the deadline hits before breakfast. Whatever is left over has to be burned up before the morning comes. I've never kept a cookie past midnight in my life, so that rule would suit me fine.
That's the one, friend. The LORD says, “before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over.” So whatever's left gets burned up before morning.
Sunset doesn't fit, baker. The LORD says, “Do not leave any of it until morning…” They slaughter the lambs at twilight, and the meal happens that night, so the deadline is morning.
Salting isn't in the instructions, friend. The LORD says any part left over must be burned up before the morning. Nothing about saving it.
Burying is a fair thought, but it's not what the LORD says. He says, “before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over.” Burn it, don't bury it.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover.” They're dressed for travel, sandals on and staff in hand, so this isn't a slow dinner. Chew fast, friend.
The LORD doesn't ask for silence here, friend. He says, “You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover.” Nothing is said about being quiet at the table.

Secret isn't the word, baker. The LORD says, “You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover.” The word He gives is haste. And the meal gets its name right there in the same line: the LORD’s Passover.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” And He says no plague will fall on them to destroy them when He strikes the land of Egypt. That's why the meal is called the Passover.

That's not how He puts it, friend. The LORD says, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.” The promise is that He passes over.
Coming back isn't mentioned, baker. The LORD says the blood will be a sign, and “when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” Passing over is the word to hold onto.

explanations.answer: For all the generations to come
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says they are to celebrate this day as a feast to the LORD, “…a permanent statute for the generations to come.” It's meant to be remembered, year after year. Even the ones who weren't there will hear about it.

explanations.answer: Until they reach the new land
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't put an end date like that on it, friend. He says they are to keep it as “…a permanent statute for the generations to come.” It keeps going long after the road ends.
It lasts much longer than that, baker. The LORD calls it “…a permanent statute for the generations to come.” One year would be a short feast, and He says this one is for the generations.

explanations.answer: He brought them out of Egypt on this day
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The LORD says, “…on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt.” That's His reason for the feast. He adds, “You must keep this day as a permanent statute for the generations to come.”

explanations.answer: He sent rain on their fields on this day
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't mentioned, friend. The LORD gives His reason: “…on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt.” That's what the feast is about.

explanations.answer: He made them a great nation on this day
explanations.explanation: Good thought, baker, but that's not what the LORD says here. His words are, “…on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt.” The feast points back to Egypt.

That's right, baker. Moses says, “Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe.” So hyssop works like a little paintbrush. A cluster of it, dipped in the basin, and the doorframe is marked.
Cedar's a fine tree, friend, but Moses names something else. He says, “Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin…” Hyssop is what they use.
No yarn in these instructions, baker. Moses says, “Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe.” The brush is hyssop.
It's the opposite, friend. Moses says, “None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning.” The blood is on the doorframe, and the family stays inside through the night.
That's right, baker. Moses says, “None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning.” Once the blood is on, everyone stays put. No midnight snack runs.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service.” The LORD made a promise about a land, and Moses says the service goes with them into it. They haven't even left Egypt yet, and Moses is already giving instructions for the other side. That's planning ahead.
A city isn't what Moses names, friend. He says, “When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service.” It's a whole land the LORD promised.
No temple comes up in this passage, baker. Moses says, “When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service.” The word he uses is land.
That's right, baker. The text says, “Then the people bowed down and worshiped.” After hearing all of this, they go low before the LORD. Sometimes that's the best answer to a big announcement.

explanations.answer: They ask Moses for a sign
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. After Moses tells the elders the Passover words, the text says, “Then the people bowed down and worshiped.” Nobody stops to ask for proof. I think after hearing what the LORD said about the Passover, bowing low just felt like the right thing to do.
Packing isn't what the text shows next, baker. It says, “Then the people bowed down and worshiped.” First comes the worship, and then, as we'll see, they do just what the LORD commanded.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). The people did what was commanded. But the story isn't over yet, so there's more still to come.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). The people did what the LORD commanded. And the story isn't over, so there's more still to come.
